concepts.name: When solutions exist
concepts.description: ax + by = c has integer solutions exactly when g = gcd(a, b) divides c. If g does not divide c, the left side is always a multiple of g and can never equal c.

concepts.name: Finding one solution
concepts.description: Make c − ax a multiple of b by trying x = 0, 1, 2, … (at most b tries), or by working with remainders on division by b.

concepts.name: The step between solutions
concepts.description: From one solution (x₀, y₀), every other is x = x₀ + (b/g)t, y = y₀ − (a/g)t: x moves by b/g and y by a/g, in opposite directions.

concepts.name: Counting solutions
concepts.description: Positive solutions need x, y ≥ 1; non-negative ones allow 0. Find the first and last solution in range and count the steps between them, plus one.

concepts.name: Coins, stamps and purchases
concepts.description: Turn a payment into a value equation such as 2x + 5y = 60. "At least one of each" means positive solutions; "any number, possibly none" means non-negative.

concepts.name: Three variables
concepts.description: x + y + z = n has C(n + 2, 2) non-negative and C(n − 1, 2) positive solutions. With unequal coefficients, fix the variable with the largest coefficient and count the rest.

concepts.name: Largest and smallest values
concepts.description: Over the solutions, x + y changes by a fixed amount each step, so its extremes are at the two ends. With coprime coins a and b, every amount above ab − a − b can be paid.

formulas.title: When ax + by = c has integer solutions
formulas.prompt: When does ax + by = c have solutions in integers?
formulas.formula: Integer solutions exist ⇔ gcd(a, b) divides c

variables.meaning: the highest common factor of a and b

formulas.explanation: ax + by is always a multiple of g = gcd(a, b). So c must be a multiple of g; and when it is, solutions always exist.
formulas.example: 6x + 9y = 20: gcd 3 does not divide 20, so no solution. 6x + 9y = 21: x = 2, y = 1.
formulas.commonMistake: Thinking the coefficients must be coprime: 9x + 12y = 102 is solvable because 3 divides 102.

formulas.title: One solution by trial
formulas.prompt: How do you find one solution of ax + by = c quickly?
formulas.formula: Try x = 0, 1, 2, …, b − 1 until b divides c − ax

variables.meaning: the coefficient you divide by (take the larger one to make trials few)

formulas.explanation: Only the remainder of ax on division by b matters, and it repeats every b values of x, so at most b tries are needed.
formulas.commonMistake: Trying values of x far beyond b; the remainders repeat after b tries.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Find a solution of 5x + 3y = 52 in positive integers.

formulas.title: The general solution
formulas.prompt: From one solution (x₀, y₀), how do you get all the others?
formulas.formula:
x = x₀ + (b/g)t
y = y₀ − (a/g)t   (t any integer, g = gcd(a, b))
formulas.explanation: Adding b/g to x adds ab/g to the left side; taking a/g from y removes the same ab/g. These are the smallest such moves.
formulas.commonMistake: Stepping x by its own coefficient a, or moving x and y the same way.
formulas.applicationPrompt: One solution of 5x + 7y = 100 is (6, 10). Find the next one.

formulas.title: Counting solutions
formulas.prompt: How do you count the solutions in positive (or non-negative) integers?

variables.meaning: the smallest and largest x that keep both variables in range

formulas.explanation: The solutions in range form an arithmetic progression in x with common difference b/g, so count the terms.
formulas.commonMistake: Forgetting the + 1, or including y = 0 when positive integers are asked for.

formulas.title: Coins and stamps
formulas.prompt: How do you set up "pay ₹T with ₹a and ₹b coins"?
formulas.formula:
ax + by = T
at least one of each → x, y ≥ 1
any number → x, y ≥ 0

variables.meaning: the numbers of each coin or stamp

formulas.explanation: The value of the coins, not their number, makes the equation; the wording decides whether 0 is allowed.
formulas.example: ₹60 with ₹2 and ₹5 coins, at least one each: 2x + 5y = 60 → y = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10 → 5 ways.
formulas.commonMistake: Counting the ways that use only one kind when "at least one of each" is asked.
formulas.applicationPrompt: In how many ways can ₹40 be paid with ₹2 and ₹5 coins, at least one of each?

formulas.title: x + y + z = n
formulas.prompt: How many solutions does x + y + z = n have?
formulas.explanation: Place 2 dividers among n items (stars and bars). For positive solutions, give each variable 1 first, leaving n − 3.
formulas.commonMistake: Using C(n, 3) or forgetting to subtract the minimums first.
formulas.applicationPrompt: How many positive solutions has x + y + z = 12?

formulas.title: Largest amount that cannot be paid
formulas.prompt: With coprime coins of ₹a and ₹b, what is the largest amount that cannot be paid exactly?
formulas.formula: Largest impossible amount = ab − a − b
formulas.explanation: Every amount above ab − a − b can be made, and ab − a − b itself cannot. If a and b share a factor, infinitely many amounts are impossible.
formulas.example: ₹3 and ₹5 coins: 15 − 8 = ₹7 is the largest that cannot be paid.
formulas.commonMistake: Using the formula when the coins share a factor (₹4 and ₹6 can never pay an odd amount).
formulas.applicationPrompt: Coins of ₹5 and ₹9: largest amount that cannot be paid?

formulas.title: Most and fewest items
formulas.prompt: Over the solutions of ax + by = c, where is x + y largest?
formulas.formula: x + y is largest with the most of the cheaper item (largest x when a < b), and smallest at the other end
formulas.explanation: Each step swaps a of the dearer items for b of the cheaper, changing the count by b − a, so the extremes sit at the ends.
formulas.example: 3x + 5y = 71: (22, 1) gives 23 stamps, the most; (2, 13) gives 15, the fewest.
formulas.commonMistake: Looking for the extreme in the middle of the list.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Pay ₹80 with ₹3 and ₹7 coins, at least one of each: most coins?

formulas.title: Work with remainders
formulas.prompt: How can remainders find x without trial?
formulas.formula: ax + by = c → ax ≡ c (mod b)

variables.meaning: same remainder on division by b

formulas.explanation: Divide everything by b and keep remainders: the by term vanishes, leaving a small equation for x.
formulas.commonMistake: Reducing by the wrong coefficient, so the unknown does not vanish.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Use remainders to find x in 4x + 9y = 100.

formulas.title: Count from the two ends
formulas.prompt: What is the quickest way to count the positive solutions once you have one?
formulas.explanation: Find the first x that works and the last x before y drops below 1, then count the arithmetic progression.
formulas.commonMistake: Dividing c by a coefficient and calling it the count.

formulas.title: Non-negative from positive
formulas.prompt: How do non-negative solutions relate to positive ones?
formulas.formula:
Non-negative solutions of ax + by = c
= positive solutions of ax + by = c + a + b

variables.meaning: x + 1 (each variable shifted up by one)

formulas.explanation: Putting x = X − 1 and y = Y − 1 turns x, y ≥ 0 into X, Y ≥ 1 and adds a + b to the right side.
formulas.example: 2x + 3y = 12 has 3 non-negative solutions; 2X + 3Y = 17 has 3 positive ones: (1, 5), (4, 3), (7, 1).
formulas.commonMistake: Adding 1 to c instead of a + b.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Turn 4x + 7y = 200 (x, y ≥ 0) into a positive-solution count.

formulas.title: Hand out the minimum first
formulas.prompt: How do you count x + y + z = n when each variable must be at least k?
formulas.formula: Give k to each first: x + y + z = n − 3k, all ≥ 0 → C(n − 3k + 2, 2)
formulas.explanation: After the minimum is handed out, what is left can be shared with no restriction.
formulas.commonMistake: Subtracting k only once instead of three times.
formulas.applicationPrompt: x + y + z = 20 with each at least 3: how many solutions?

levels.title: Lattice Points on a Line
levels.description: When ax + by = c has whole-number solutions, how to find one, and the steady step from one solution to the next.

blocks.title: Only multiples of the gcd can be reached
blocks.body: 4x + 6y is even for every pair of integers, so 4x + 6y = 15 has no solution at all. In general ax + by is always a multiple of g = gcd(a, b), and every multiple of g can be reached. So ax + by = c has integer solutions exactly when g divides c.

blocks.title: Find one, then step
blocks.body:
To solve 7x + 5y = 96 in positive integers, make 96 − 7x a multiple of 5. x = 1 gives 89, x = 2 gives 82, x = 3 gives 75 ✓, so (3, 15) is a solution.

Now raise x by 5 and lower y by 7: the left side gains 35 and loses 35, so it stays 96. That gives (8, 8) and (13, 1). One more step would make y negative, so there are exactly 3 positive solutions.

blocks.title: Every solution from one
blocks.caption: x steps by the other coefficient, y by its own partner’s, in opposite directions. Divide by g = gcd(a, b) first: 4x + 6y = 40 steps by 3 and 2, not 6 and 4.

blocks.body: "Positive integers" means x, y ≥ 1; "non-negative" allows 0. The two counts differ exactly by the end points where x = 0 or y = 0, so read the question for "at least one of each".

levels.title: Integer Solution Formulas
levels.description: When solutions exist, one solution, the general solution, counting and coin problems.

levels.title: Direct Integer Solutions
levels.description: Decide whether solutions exist, find one, and take one step.

levels.title: Counting and Coins
levels.description: Count positive and non-negative solutions and set up coin and stamp problems.

levels.title: Ranges, Counts and Purchases
levels.description: Multi-step counting, purchases with an extra condition, and the full method in order.

levels.title: Advanced: Three Unknowns and Extremes
levels.description: Share n things among three people, count ax + y + z = n, find the most or fewest items, and the largest amount two coins cannot pay.

blocks.title: Three unknowns: dividers among items
blocks.body:
x + y + z = 10 in non-negative integers is 10 items and 2 dividers in a row: choose where the 2 dividers go among 12 places, C(12, 2) = 66 ways. If each must be at least 1, hand out 1 each first: x + y + z = 7 with no limit, C(9, 2) = 36.

With a larger coefficient, as in 2x + y + z = 12, fix x = 0, 1, …, 6 and count y + z = 12 − 2x each time: 13 + 11 + 9 + 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 49.

blocks.title: Extremes sit at the ends
blocks.body: For 3x + 5y = 71 the solutions are (2, 13), (7, 10), (12, 7), (17, 4), (22, 1). Each step trades 3 five-rupee stamps for 5 three-rupee ones, adding 2 to the count, so the most stamps is at the end with the largest x: 23. The fewest is at the other end: 15.

blocks.title: Amounts two coins cannot pay
blocks.body: Largest impossible amount = ab − a − b   (gcd(a, b) = 1)
blocks.caption: With ₹3 and ₹5 coins, ₹7 is the last amount that cannot be paid; ₹8, ₹9 and ₹10 can, and adding ₹3 coins reaches everything after.

blocks.body: If the two coins share a factor, the formula does not apply: ₹4 and ₹6 coins can never pay an odd amount, however large.

levels.title: Challenge: Sharing, Coins and Extremes
levels.description: Three-variable counts, the largest unpayable amount, and the most or fewest items.

questions.question: Which of these equations has no solution in integers?
questions.explanation: 4x + 6y = 2(2x + 3y) is even for every pair of integers, and 15 is odd, so it can never hold. The others work: 3(−1) + 5(2) = 7, 6(2) + 9(1) = 21 and 2(2) + 7(1) = 11.
questions.method: Check whether gcd(a, b) divides c.

hints.text: Find the gcd of the two coefficients in each equation.
Can an even number ever equal 15?

commonMistakes: Ruling out 6x + 9y = 21 because 6 and 9 share a factor; 3 divides 21, so it is solvable.

questions.question: x and y are positive integers with 7x + 5y = 96. What is the smallest possible value of x?
questions.explanation: 96 − 7x must be a positive multiple of 5. x = 1 gives 89, x = 2 gives 82, x = 3 gives 75 = 5 × 15. So the smallest x is 3, with y = 15.
questions.method: Try x = 1, 2, … until 96 − 7x is a multiple of 5.

hints.text: For y to be whole, 96 − 7x must end in 0 or 5.
7x must end in 1 or 6.

commonMistakes: Giving the smallest y (1, at x = 13) instead of the smallest x.

questions.question: x = 4, y = 11 is a solution of 3x + 8y = 100. Which is the next solution in positive integers with a larger x?
questions.explanation: gcd(3, 8) = 1, so x steps by 8 and y by 3, in opposite directions: (4 + 8, 11 − 3) = (12, 8). Check: 36 + 64 = 100.
solutionSteps: x goes up by the other coefficient, 8.
questions.method: x moves by b/g, y by a/g, in opposite directions.

hints.text: If x goes up, which way must y go to keep the total at 100?
Adding 8 to x adds 24; take 3 from y to remove 24.

commonMistakes: Stepping x by its own coefficient 3 and y by 8, which gives (7, 3) and a total of 45.

questions.question: 2x + 3y = 12 has exactly one solution in positive integers.
questions.explanation: The non-negative solutions are (0, 4), (3, 2) and (6, 0). Only (3, 2) has both values at least 1, so there is exactly one positive solution: true.
questions.method: List the solutions and drop those with a zero.

hints.text: y can only be 0, 2 or 4 (12 − 3y must be even).
Which of those also give x ≥ 1?

commonMistakes: Counting (0, 4) and (6, 0), which are non-negative but not positive.

questions.question: (x₀, y₀) is one solution of ax + by = c, and g = gcd(a, b). Which formula gives every integer solution?

options.text: x = x₀ + t, y = y₀ − t

questions.explanation: Adding b/g to x adds ab/g to the left side; taking a/g from y removes the same ab/g, so the total stays c. These are the smallest such moves, so every solution is reached.
questions.method: Each variable steps by the other’s coefficient over g, in opposite directions.

hints.text: Raising x must be balanced by lowering y.
x is multiplied by a, so its step must be the other coefficient.

commonMistakes: Stepping x by a/g: the change a²/g in the left side is not cancelled by b²/g unless a = b.

questions.question: How many solutions in positive integers does 3x + 5y = 100 have?
questions.explanation: 100 − 3x must be a multiple of 5, so x is a multiple of 5: x = 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 give y = 17, 14, 11, 8, 5, 2. x = 35 would give y = −1. That is 6 solutions.
solutionSteps: 100 and 5y are multiples of 5, so 3x is too: x = 5k.
questions.method: First and last solution, then count the steps.

hints.text: Which values of x make 100 − 3x a multiple of 5?
x = 5 is the first; x rises by 5 while y falls by 3.

commonMistakes: Including x = 0 (y = 20), which is not positive, to get 7.

questions.question: Ananya wants to pay exactly ₹60 at a toll booth using only ₹2 and ₹5 coins, with at least one coin of each kind. In how many ways can she do it?
questions.explanation: 2x + 5y = 60 with x, y ≥ 1. 5y must be even, so y = 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, giving x = 25, 20, 15, 10, 5. y = 12 would leave x = 0. So 5 ways.
questions.method: Value equation, then positive solutions.

hints.text: Let x = number of ₹2 coins and y = number of ₹5 coins.
60 − 5y must be even, so y is even.

commonMistakes: Allowing all ₹2 coins (y = 0) or all ₹5 coins (x = 0), giving 7.

questions.question: How many pairs of non-negative integers (x, y) satisfy 4x + 7y = 200?
questions.explanation: 7y must be a multiple of 4, so y = 0, 4, 8, …, 28, giving x = 50, 43, 36, …, 1. y = 32 would make x negative. That is 28 ÷ 4 + 1 = 8 pairs.
solutionSteps: 200 − 7y divisible by 4 → y a multiple of 4.
questions.method: Non-negative: both ends (0 allowed) count.

hints.text: Which y make 200 − 7y a multiple of 4?
y can be 0 here.

commonMistakes: Leaving out y = 0, which non-negative allows, to get 7.

questions.question: 9x + 12y = 102 has no solution in integers, because 9 and 12 are not coprime.
questions.explanation: gcd(9, 12) = 3 and 102 = 3 × 34, so solutions exist: x = 2, y = 7 gives 18 + 84 = 102. Coefficients that share a factor only matter when that factor does not divide c: false.
questions.method: The test is whether gcd(a, b) divides c, not whether a and b are coprime.

hints.text: Divide the whole equation by 3.
Does 3x + 4y = 34 have a solution?

commonMistakes: Thinking only coprime coefficients give solutions.

questions.question: Meena buys ₹3 and ₹5 postage stamps for exactly ₹71, at least one of each. How many different combinations of stamps could she have bought?
questions.explanation: 3x + 5y = 71 with x, y ≥ 1. 71 − 5y must be a multiple of 3: y = 1, 4, 7, 10, 13 give x = 22, 17, 12, 7, 2. y = 16 would need 80 > 71. So 5 combinations.
questions.method: One solution, then step y by 3 and x by 5.

hints.text: Start with y = 1: is 71 − 5 a multiple of 3?
Then y rises by 3 while x falls by 5.

commonMistakes: Stepping y by 5 instead of 3.

questions.question: Which pair (x, y) of positive integers satisfies 11x + 4y = 101?
questions.method: Substitute, or use remainders on division by 4.

hints.text: 101 is odd and 4y is even, so 11x must be odd.
Try odd x: which makes 101 − 11x a multiple of 4?

commonMistakes: Accepting (7, 5) as close enough: it gives 97, not 101.

questions.question: A school canteen buys pens at ₹7 each and notebooks at ₹12 each, spending exactly ₹250 and buying at least one of each. It bought more notebooks than pens. How many pens did it buy?
questions.explanation: 7x + 12y = 250. 250 − 12y must be a multiple of 7: y = 1 gives 238 = 7 × 34. So the solutions are (34, 1), (22, 8) and (10, 15), stepping x by 12 and y by 7. Only (10, 15) has more notebooks than pens: 10 pens.
questions.method: List every positive solution, then apply the extra condition.

hints.text: Find one solution first: try y = 1.
x steps by 12 and y by 7. Which solution has y > x?

commonMistakes: Stopping at the first solution found (34 pens), which has fewer notebooks.

questions.question: How many pairs of non-negative integers satisfy 5x + 8y = 200?
questions.explanation: 200 − 8y must be a multiple of 5, so y is a multiple of 5: y = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 give x = 40, 32, 24, 16, 8, 0. That is 6 pairs; the 4 with both values positive leave out the two ends.
solutionSteps: y must be a multiple of 5.
y = 0 to 25 in steps of 5: x = 40 down to 0.
questions.method: Both ends count when zero is allowed.

hints.text: Which y make 200 − 8y a multiple of 5?
Both (40, 0) and (0, 25) are allowed here.

commonMistakes: Counting only positive solutions (4).
Dividing 200 by 8 to get 25.

questions.question: x and y are positive integers with 13x + 9y = 500. What is the difference between the largest and the smallest possible value of x?
questions.explanation: 500 − 13x must be a multiple of 9. 500 leaves 5 on division by 9 and 13 leaves 4, so 4x must leave 5: x = 8 (32 leaves 5). Then x = 8, 17, 26, 35 with y = 44, 31, 18, 5; x = 44 would make y negative. The difference is 35 − 8 = 27.
questions.method: Smallest x by remainders, then step by 9 while y stays positive.

hints.text: Work with remainders on division by 9.
x steps by 9; how many steps fit before y drops below 1?

commonMistakes: Taking x up to 44, which makes y negative.

questions.question: Select ALL the equations that have exactly three solutions in positive integers.
questions.method: Count each one from its first and last solution.

hints.text: Find the first solution of each, then step.
In 2x + 5y = 31, y must be odd.

commonMistakes: Counting end points with a zero, such as (10, 0) for 3x + 4y = 30, which are not positive.

questions.question: Match each equation with the number of its solutions in positive integers.
questions.method: First solution, step, count.

hints.text: Find the first solution of each.
Count how many steps keep both values at least 1.

commonMistakes: Counting (0, 10) and (25, 0) for 2x + 5y = 50 and getting 6.

questions.question: Put the steps in order to count the positive integer solutions of 7x + 5y = 96.

steps.text: Check that gcd(7, 5) = 1 divides 96, so solutions exist
Write the step: x goes up by 5 while y goes down by 7
Step until y would drop below 1: (8, 8), (13, 1)

questions.explanation: Existence first, then one solution, then the step, then the end of the range, then the count. Without one solution there is nothing to step from.
questions.method: Exists → one solution → step → range → count.

hints.text: You cannot step until you have one solution.
Checking the gcd comes before any search.

commonMistakes: Stepping by 7 in x (its own coefficient).

questions.question: In how many ways can 10 identical laddoos be shared among three children so that each child gets at least one?
questions.explanation: Give each child one laddoo first; 7 remain to be shared with no limit. x + y + z = 7 in non-negative integers has C(7 + 2, 2) = C(9, 2) = 36 solutions. (Directly: C(10 − 1, 2) = 36.)
solutionSteps: Hand out 1 each: x′ + y′ + z′ = 7, each ≥ 0.
questions.method: Remove the minimums, then stars and bars.

hints.text: Write x + y + z = 10 with x, y, z ≥ 1.
Positive solutions of x + y + z = n: C(n − 1, 2).

commonMistakes: Using C(12, 2) = 66, which allows a child to get none.

questions.question: A vending machine at a railway station accepts only ₹5 and ₹8 coins and gives no change. What is the largest whole-rupee price that cannot be paid exactly?
questions.explanation: 5 and 8 are coprime, so the largest amount that cannot be made is 5 × 8 − 5 − 8 = 27. Check: 27, 19, 11 and 3 (27 minus 0 to 3 eights) are not multiples of 5, so 27 fails; 28 = 20 + 8, 29 = 5 + 24, 30, 31 = 15 + 16 and 32 all work, and adding ₹5 coins reaches everything after.
solutionSteps: 28, 29, 30, 31, 32 are all payable, so everything above is too.
questions.method: ab − a − b for coprime coins.

hints.text: Every large enough amount can be paid. Where does the run of payable amounts begin?
For coprime a and b the answer is ab − a − b.

commonMistakes: Answering 5 × 8 = 40, or 39.

questions.question: How many solutions in non-negative integers does 2x + y + z = 12 have?
questions.explanation: x can be 0 to 6. For each x, y + z = 12 − 2x has 13 − 2x non-negative solutions: 13 + 11 + 9 + 7 + 5 + 3 + 1 = 49.
questions.method: Fix the variable with the larger coefficient and add up.

hints.text: Try x = 0, 1, 2, … in turn.
y + z = m has m + 1 non-negative solutions.

commonMistakes: Using C(14, 2) = 91 as if every coefficient were 1.

questions.question: Meena spends exactly ₹71 on ₹3 and ₹5 stamps, buying at least one of each. What is the largest number of stamps she can buy?
questions.explanation: 3x + 5y = 71 has positive solutions (2, 13), (7, 10), (12, 7), (17, 4), (22, 1), with x three-rupee stamps. Each step swaps 3 five-rupee stamps for 5 three-rupee ones, adding 2 stamps. So the most is 22 + 1 = 23.
questions.method: Most items → most of the cheaper item.

hints.text: Use as many ₹3 stamps as possible.
She still needs at least one ₹5 stamp.

commonMistakes: Giving 15, the fewest.
Dividing 71 by 5 to get 14.

questions.question: With an unlimited supply of ₹3 and ₹7 coins, every whole-rupee amount from ₹12 upwards can be paid exactly.
questions.explanation: gcd(3, 7) = 1, so the largest amount that cannot be paid is 3 × 7 − 3 − 7 = 11. ₹12 = 4 × 3, ₹13 = 2 × 3 + 7, ₹14 = 2 × 7, and adding ₹3 coins reaches everything after: true.
solutionSteps: Adding 3 repeatedly covers the rest: true.
questions.method: ab − a − b is the last amount that fails.

hints.text: Find the largest amount ₹3 and ₹7 coins cannot make.
Three payable amounts in a row, plus ₹3 coins, cover everything above.

commonMistakes: Thinking ₹11 can be paid (11 − 7 = 4 is not a multiple of 3).

questions.question: How many solutions does x + y + z = 15 have if x, y and z are whole numbers, each at least 2?
questions.explanation: Give 2 to each first: x′ + y′ + z′ = 15 − 6 = 9 with no limit, which has C(9 + 2, 2) = C(11, 2) = 55 solutions.
questions.method: Hand out the minimum, then stars and bars.

hints.text: Set x = x′ + 2 and so on.
Then count non-negative solutions of a smaller sum.

commonMistakes: Ignoring the minimum (C(17, 2) = 136).
Using the at-least-one count (C(14, 2) = 91).
